item.title: Disable this Windows 11 setting for a faster, longer-lasting laptop
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
The modern look of Windows 11 relies heavily on what is known as ‘Fluent Design,’ with transparent menus and smooth animations. It looks stylish, but it takes up processing power. According to Microsoft’s documentation, rendering certain glass effects — such as the so-called ‘Acrylic’ material — is GPU-intensive and can slow down system performance on older PCs or laptops, as well as putting greater strain on your battery. Foundry If you’re using less powerful hardware or simply want a more responsive system, you can disable these effects in just a few clicks: Disable transparency effects: Press Win + I to open Settings and navigate to Personalization > Colors (or Accessibility > Visual effects ). There, toggle off the switch for Transparency effects . This will make the display look a little simpler and may result in smoother performance on less powerful hardware. Disable animations: Under Settings > Accessibility > Visual effects , you can also turn off Animation effects . This means that, amongst other things, Windows will no longer display animated transitions when opening, minimizing or moving windows, nor will it show other motion effects in the interface. Menus and windows will then appear without these brief transitions, which can make the interface feel more immediate and responsive. A classic performance tweak via the Control Panel Foundry You can also disable further visual effects in Windows. To do this , type ‘Adjust Windows appearance and performance’ into the search box on the taskbar and open the corresponding entry. Go to the Visual Effects tab and select Adjust for best performance . Windows will then disable various animations and other visual effects, which can make the system run more smoothly on less powerful hardware. Even more performance bottlenecks lie dormant in the Autostart folder on older PCs. Open Task Manager using Ctrl + Shift + Esc and go to ‘Startup apps .’ You can disable any programs you don’t need there. These will then no longer be loaded automatically by Windows at start-up. You can re-enable these start-up programs at any time from here. Note: Don’t expect these settings to provide a massive performance boost — on modern gaming PCs, the effect is negligible. On older laptops or mini PCs, however, disabling these visual effects can result in smoother performance or longer battery life. For a relatively low price, this build beats a standard budget mini PC by miles. GMKtec Mini AI PC , Intel Core Ultra 5 226V/16GB DDR5 RAM—$550 (29% off on Amazon) At 29 percent off, this GMKtec mini PC is an appealing option if you want one of Intel’s newer Core Ultra chips. The Core Ultra 5 226V gives you good all-around performance along with Intel’s newer integrated graphics and AI hardware. It’s a versatile little system for productivity, media, and lighter creative workloads. And with 16GB of DDR5 memory included, it has enough horsepower for most home and office setups. What should you look for when buying a mini PC? The first thing you have to check off your list is just what configuration you need to get your job done. Are you going to use your new mini PC for browsing only? Then a cheap budget-friendly device with a decent CPU and 16GB of RAM will do the trick. Do you want to do some light gaming in your downtime? Look for a device that comes with a GPU or Occulink connectivity to hook up an external GPU instead. Are you looking to utilize the mini PC as a home server? Your priority then should be a large SSD—2TB or more. There are devices for each and every one of these scenarios, and they’re all quite affordable. The best part is that mini PCs are… well, small, so they can be placed practically anywhere depending on your intended use and available space. They also support multiple monitors out of the box, which makes it easy to replace your old, larger desktop and you won’t even need to pay for extra hubs. 2. Can a mini PC replace a desktop computer? For most people, the answer is “yes”! Mini PCs are definitely powerful enough to replace desktops for most users, especially if you’re going to use it for work, browsing, or streaming movies. If you want something for photo and video editing, or even gaming, there are models that allow you to do that, but they’ll cost a bit more. But it will ultimately depend upon the mini PC you buy and which modern games you want to play. Some high-performance mini PCs can run modern AAA games. You might not be able to run them at the highest settings though, and performance will depend heavily on the specific hardware. If you do want to game on a mini PC, look for powerful models with dedicated discrete GPUs such as an Nvidia RTX or AMD Radeon rather than integrated graphics. Alternatively, you can opt for cloud streaming services to game on less powerful mini PCs, which bypasses the need for high-end hardware. 4. Which mini PC brands are reliable? Some of the most reliable mini PC brands are Minisforum, Beelink, GMKtec, and Geekom. Of course Apple’s Mac minis are also excellent computers if you prefer using macOS. Brands such as Asus, Lenovo, HP, and Dell all make high-quality smaller-footprint PCs, but they might not fill the same niche and/or they are typically more expensive.

item.title: What does Amazon know about you? The answer is buried in your account info
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
We all know companies profile us. But understanding that abstractly is one thing. Reading the words “has flat buttocks” in your Amazon account is very much another. If you’re not on Threads, this discovery is one of the latest viral posts . A woman stumbled upon this assumption while in her Amazon settings, buried among other, less inflammatory ones within the Your Shopping preferences section. Of course, having read that post myself while doomscrolling before bed, I resolved to look at my own profile in the morning. (I have a vested interested in privacy as a topic, after all.) Turns out, Amazon has little incendiary commentary about me. You might even say I’m boring. Here’s how you look it up. On a desktop PC, head to Account . Under Ordering and shopping preferences , click on Your shopping preferences . Then look for Manage your information at the bottom of the page. You should then see a page titled About You , listing details that Amazon says it uses to “personalize your experience for you and everyone you shop for.” Amazon / PCWorld For me, Amazon believes I like technology and photography. And I prefer Command strips for mounting hardware. That’s about it. As you might guess, these assumptions are based on your shopping habits—and surprisingly upfront. (Finding the equivalent information on Facebook feels like a labyrinth of clicks, and the details aren’t as blunt as “has flat buttocks.”) As disappointed as I am Amazon’s spiciest commentary on me was “prefers white networking cables,” I got a good lesson from looking up my profile. One, it confirms that where and how you shop affects the data that businesses collect. Two, it’s a good reminder that I should keep looking up these details on different websites and services. And three, this will only get more complicated as agentic AI services pull in and collate data about us through friends, family, and associates.

item.title: The Surface Laptop Ultra is an AI monster with a laptop problem
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Microsoft’s new Surface Laptop Ultra is powered by a Mediatek CPU and Nvidia’s powerful RTX Spark SoC, which is mainly designed to run local AI models on the user’s lap. Five competing laptops—from Dell, HP, MSI and more—will offer additional options. Here’s the thinking. Microsoft is banking on near-future AI developers and enthusiasts running local AI models and tools directly from their PC. If needed, they’ll tap Microsoft’s Copilot AI for more horsepower. Microsoft calls this “hybrid intelligence” and it’s basically an acknowledgement that users won’t necessarily care which device does what. It’s a compromise, as is most anything that’s AI-related in productivity: some love it, others despise it. There are further tradeoffs. Users will be able to run models locally, but the Surface Laptop Ultra ships with a 140W power adapter. That’s a signal that it will consume much more power than typical laptops, though not gaming laptops. (That’s another question: is this a gaming laptop? Microsoft showed just a single Gears of War game running on the Ultra, with no indication of frame rate.) Nevertheless, I left the Windows and Surface Event with a question that no one at Microsoft could answer: What will be the battery life of these laptops? In one demonstration, Microsoft employee Kayla Cinnamon proudly put the Surface Laptop Ultra into “airplane mode,” showing how the laptop could run entirely disconnected from a network. (Microsoft’s official stance: “Battery life details for Surface Laptop Ultra will be shared closer to availability,” reads the Ultra’s spec page . “It varies based on usage, settings, configuration, and other factors.”) But these laptops may not even work on airplanes. For one, 140W is more than some airplane power outlets can supply—110W to 150W is apparently typical. (Edit: Jason Rabinowitz, cohost of the AVTalk podcast and an avid airline enthusiast, says that 60 to 100 watts is actually more common.) Will you be able to run AI agents continuously throughout a 13-hour flight from San Francisco to Taiwan? I very much doubt it. We don’t even have a reliable way to test the battery life while churning tokens. All of these unknowns left the analysts I spoke to shaking their heads. Who’s going to buy these devices? The $2,599 price is the base, which means as users scale up to more and more memory—to run larger and more powerful AI models—the price will balloon with it. We’re still in 2026, a time when the $699 Apple MacBook Neo blew up headlines. “I think it’s very obvious that no one wants to spend all this crazy money [on cloud AI],” said analyst Bob O’Donnell, principal at Technalysis. But how users want to divvy up their work between slower local AI and faster, more expensive cloud models remains to be seen. It seems we have a new breed of laptops that might not really be laptops at all—they may not have the battery to last with how much power they chug, and they can’t plug in while on the go. They’re “portable” AI workstations for a niche of users who are willing to pay more than what it costs for a normal productivity laptop, for “productivity” loathed by some of its users. Whew. Updated at 2:02 PM with additional detail.

Read our full Plugable USB-C Triple 4K HDMI and DisplayPort Display Horizontal Docking Station (UD-6950PDZ) review Other USB-C hub/dock reviews and features Anker Nano 13-in-1 USB-C dock review: This combo USB-C dock/hub doesn’t deliver the amount of charging power I’d hope for, though the two-for-one special is unique. Mokin 160W GaN All-in-One Station : With great power comes great…performance. Ugreen’s $5 cable deal: Deals come and go, but check back for an attractive price. USB-C buying guide : Our friends at PCWelt have some advice on how to differentiate USB from Thunderbolt. How we test USB-C hubs We test USB-C hubs/dongles slightly differently than docking stations. A separate article offers a detailed explanation on how we test USB-C hubs , but here’s a short summary: First we test the physical configuration, and how ports are spaced and whether filling one port impedes use of the port next to it. We also run performance tests to make sure ports function as advertised. Finally, we consider price and weight it against functionality and build quality. More complex hubs usually command more money, but that’s not always the case! Who curated this article? My name is Mark Hachman , and I’ve been working as a technology reporter and reviewer for 30 years. I review USB-C hubs/dongles, Thunderbolt docking stations, and DisplayLink docks, so I have a good handle on the different types of I/O technologies being used and what will be best for you. I’ve been reviewing these devices since work-from-home became popular in 2020, realizing pretty quickly that home users wanted a mix of displays and legacy peripherals. How to choose the best USB-C hub You’ll want to do a careful of assessment of your work equipment and your needs in order to find the right hub or dock for yourself. First, take stock of your peripherals Here’s where to start: Take a look at the peripherals you own, or plan to buy. Do you have an old external hard drive that uses a traditional USB-A cable? Do you manually back up photos from an SLR camera via its SD card? Or is your Wi-Fi connection unreliable enough that you’d prefer Ethernet? Figure out what ports you’ll need. This advice is for Windows users; Macs have their own limitations on USB-C connections. Keep in mind that you may want to use both a mouse and keyboard, and possibly connect a printer, too. You can disconnect a keyboard to print, but it’s kind of a pain. Even if you own a modern 2026 laptop, you may still have hardware from several years ago. A hub bridges your laptop to its peripherals, but can serve as a bridge to the past, too. This laptop has several USB-C ports, but if yours has just one, you’ll want to daisy-chain the laptop’s power cord by plugging it directly into the hub, like so. Next, check out what ports your laptop already has It’s also important to take stock of your laptop or tablet’s ports: Does it have one USB-C port or two? If your device only has one port, is there a separate charging connection? If your laptop or tablet has a USB-C port and uses it exclusively for charging , you’ll want to buy a USB-C hub with a dedicated charging input port. Note how much input power the port allows, and confirm that it will be sufficient for your laptop. Otherwise, you’ll be forced to choose between charging your laptop and accessing other devices, which makes little sense. Most laptops will pop up a warning about a “slow charger” if your laptop’s not getting enough juice. A laptop’s USB-C port. Matt Smith/IDG Video adds another wrinkle. Older laptops often included dedicated video ports, often HDMI; modern laptops in 2026 may include a dedicated video port as well. But video can also run over the USB-C port through a technology called DP Alt Mode which enables certain USB-C ports to send video signals to external monitors using the DisplayPort protocol, via the USB-C cable. The problem, even as manufacturers like BenQ admit , is that these cables aren’t often properly labeled. There’s no way for us to tell you whether your USB-C port can support video passing over it. You’ll need to consult your laptop’s manual to tell. If the port does support video, you can either use a USB-C hub to connect to an external monitor. Alternatively, you can run the USB-C cable to a display with a USB-C cable input. These USB-C displays have only been available for a few years, but they provide an alternate way of routing video out of your laptop. Assess your laptop and peripheral power needs Desktop hubs will often take power in from an external charger like the one you plug into your phone, and use it to power your laptop. On these hubs or dongles, there will be a dedicated USB-C input port to accept power, but not data. A powered laptop docking station, on the other hand, ships with its own charger — which may be hardwired into the docking station and take will power in and also push it out to peripherals. As I noted above, the input power to your laptop needs to be sufficient to power it. But if you’re investing in a powered USB-C docking station, check our reviews to see how much power the hub or docking station can push out to peripherals. The 2026 iPhone 17 Max consumes 40W of charging power to fast-charge the phone; most docking stations won’t get near that. But an older phone, such as an Apple iPhone 14, only needed 30W of charging power. Older phones need even less power to fast-charge them. You certainly don’t have to buy a USB-C docking station or hub to charge a phone; most hubs weren’t built with them in mind. It’s useful to know, however, what your hub or docking station will be able to do or not do. Making sense of the USB-C technologies A USB-C port on your laptop can either run at 5Gbps or 10Gbps, with the latter being almost ubiquitous these days. That’s plenty of bandwidth for a printer, a mouse, a keyboard, or a hard drive, even all at once. Products like displays, Ethernet, and high-speed SSDs gobble up that bandwidth, however. Display technologies tend to have the most influence over what you should buy. If you simply want to connect to an external 1080p display — or two — a USB-C dongle should work fine, provided that the dongle has the available ports. It’s certainly the cheapest option. If you want to connect more displays with higher resolution, you may have to examine other choices. Traditionally, the only other alternative was a Thunderbolt dock . Provided your laptop had a Thunderbolt port, Thunderbolt’s 40Gbps bandwidth allows for two 4K displays, running at 60Hz, plus various peripherals. (You can use a 10Gbps USB-C dock even if you have a 40Gbps Thunderbolt port, but only 10Gbps of that throughput will be available to the 10Gbps dock.) Thunderbolt is usually associated with laptops which use Intel processors; laptops with AMD Ryzen or Qualcomm Snapdragon chips inside use the “generic” equivalent, also called USB4. There are also two intermediary technologies to choose from: a DisplayLink USB-C dock, and a USB-C dock that takes advantage of something called HBR3 and DSC. DisplayLink , owned by Synaptics, uses software compression between your laptop and the dock to approximate a Thunderbolt experience over a generic USB-C connection. It requires a software driver, but our experience is that it’s an excellent choice for office work, but not gaming. Here are the best DisplayLink docks and why to buy them. HBR3 with Display Compression ( HBR3 with DSC ) is essentially an industry standard version of DisplayLink. The problem? The technology hasn’t been widely publicized, let alone supported. Our experience has been that docks that support HBR3 work well with laptops using 12th-gen Core processors on up. Laptops with a 10th-gen Core chip inside them aren’t supported, and 11th-gen Core laptops are iffy. If you own a laptop chip with a 12th-gen Core chip or one that’s even more recent, you stand a good chance of success. Otherwise, don’t bother. Thunderbolt cables and ports include the little lightning-bolt icon, which differentiates them from the otherwise unmarked USB-C cables. Finally, don’t worry about platform branding Because USB-C is common among Macs, Windows PCs, and phones, some hubs align their branding with a particular platform. Go ahead and use that USB-C that’s billed as being “for MacBook Pro, Chromebook, and XPS” with any Windows PC — we did, and it works just fine. You won’t need any special software or drivers. After testing our USB-C hubs, we can confirm that some no-names perform just as well as their more well-known counterparts, and for less money, too. One thing to keep in mind: Because price is so critical to our recommendations, know that some of the prices may change as manufacturers offer sales. Therefore some hubs we didn’t recommend primarily based on price could become more purchase-worthy. FAQ 1. Why buy a USB-C hub or dongle? Remember when laptops used to contain all sorts of ports: USB-A, HDMI, SD card slots, and more? And do you remember how svelte the early Macintosh laptops looked, especially when Apple began removing all of the ports in favor of USB-C and Thunderbolt? PC makers did, and decided that was the approach that they would take, too. Unfortunately, that left laptop owners like you with the problem of legacy hardware: printers, keyboards, SD card, micro SD cards, and so on — and with no ports to plug them into. Enter the USB-C hub, an inexpensive product that helps solve that problem. Just pay attention to what ports the USB-C hub offers, to make sure it meets your needs. 2. I don’t understand what the difference is between a USB-C hub, a DisplayLink dock, and a Thunderbolt docking station. What do I need? Here’s the short answer: If you want to connect your laptop to a printer, an SD card or microSD card, mouse, keyboard, or legacy 1080p monitor, stick with a basic 10Gbps USB-C hub/dongle. If you want to add a pair of additional displays (especially 4K), or high-speed SSD drives, we’d recommend you look at our list of 40Gbps Thunderbolt docking stations . Generally, the larger, powered docks offer more features. It is confusing, since they all use the “same” USB-C port. Generally, most modern laptops have a small Thunderbolt “lightning bolt” logo to help distinguish the faster port. 3. What’s the difference between a USB-C hub, USB-C dongle, and a USB-C docking station? A USB-C hub or dongle (we use the terms interchangeably) is a small, portable device that you can slide into a bag or backpack. A USB-C docking station tends to be heavy and bulky enough that you’ll want to keep it on your desk. It’s not true that a USB-C docking station will have more features than a USB-C hub, as some compact USB-C hubs pack in a surprising number of ports. Docking stations tend to be bigger and bulkier, and are designed to live on your desk. If there’s anything that docking stations tend to have that dongles sometimes don’t, it’s a USB-C port designed only to accept power from your laptop’s USB-C charger. That allows you to gain additional ports as well as charging capabilities from the same dock. 4. How much does a USB-C hub or dongle cost? Expect to pay between $30 and $40 for a good USB-C hub, even in 2026 — maybe a bit more with tariffs. USB-C docking stations are bigger and bulkier but add even more capabilities. We’d expect you to pay over $100 for these. 5. How much does price matter when buying a USB-C hub or dongle? Honestly, not much. Pay attention to our reviews and those from other shoppers, but buy according to what the hub or dongle offers. You can absolutely find solid USB-C hubs and dongles for an inexpensive price. USB-C docking stations , though, can feel a bit overpriced. In part, that’s because Thunderbolt docks were wildly expensive during the 2020 to 2021 pandemic years. USB-C docking stations are an alternative, but their prices were nudged upward, too. Fortunately, prices have come down, as the supply chain regained a semblance of normalcy. 6. What is the difference between USB-C and Thunderbolt? Both USB-C and Thunderbolt use the same USB-C connection. The difference is that a “generic” USB-C connection typically provides 10Gbps of bandwidth, and Thunderbolt provides 40Gbps, or 120Gbps with Thunderbolt 5 . Thunderbolt ports are becoming much more common, so it’s possible that your laptop won’t have any “USB-C” ports; they’ll be Thunderbolt-enabled instead. (To tell the difference, consult your laptop’s manual or look for a small “lightning bolt” logo over the port itself. That’s usually a sign that it’s a Thunderbolt port.) A USB-C dongle and a Thunderbolt dock are similar, in that they both provide a number of additional ports. There’s a key difference, though. The rule of thumb is that a USB-C dongle provides enough bandwidth for two 1080p displays at 60Hz, or a single 4K display at 30Hz. (Staring at any 30Hz display for a length of time can tire out your eyes, so I don’t recommend it.) A Thunderbolt dock, however, allows enough bandwidth to connect two 4K displays at 60Hz, plus all the peripherals you wish to attach. If you don’t need big, high-resolution displays, don’t buy a Thunderbolt dock and purchase a USB-C hub instead. 7. What’s a DisplayLink USB-C dock? A DisplayLink USB-C dock is what you might call a “tweener” device: something between USB-C and Thunderbolt. DisplayLink docks embed a small chip from Synaptics in the docking station, and require use of a software driver that you’ll need to download. (USB-C and Thunderbolt are essentially plug and play.) The Synaptics chip compresses the data, and gives you the ability to connect (no joke) up to three or sometimes four 4K display all over a 10Gbps USB-C cable. It feels a bit like black magic. They’re not foolproof; DisplayLink docks are best for office work (email, Word, Excel, and so on that don’t require a whole lot of bandwidth, because the images are largely static) and web browsing. Transfer a lot of data (or play back a lot of high-bitrate video) and you’ll see some stuttering. We used to break out DisplayLink docks into their own page, but we now include recommendations on this list of the best USB-C hubs, as well as our list of the best Thunderbolt docks . If you shop smart, you can get the capabilities of a Thunderbolt dock, for less. 8. Can you connect a USB-C dongle to a Thunderbolt dock? Or to another USB-C hub? You can absolutely connect a USB-C hub to a Thunderbolt dock. You probably won’t be able to connect a USB-C dongle to another USB-C dongle/hub, but if your laptop has more than one USB-C port, you can connect a USB-C hub to each. Thunderbolt offers the ability to “daisy-chain” devices, however, so you can connect one Thunderbolt dock to another. USB-C, however, does not. 9. Why do USB-C hubs get so hot? USB-C hubs can get warm or even hot while using them to transfer data or charge devices. This is because the electronic components and circuitry within hubs build up heat during use. Depending upon the hub’s material, heat can become trapped inside the hub leading it to become hot to the touch. If you are concerned about your hub becoming too hot during use, you may consider purchasing a hub made from metallic parts, such as aluminum, so that heat can more easily dissipate as it builds up. Even though two USB-C hubs may have wildly different brand names, you may sometimes find that they’re otherwise identical or just very similar. We’ve given you a lot of detail on what makes a good USB-C hub or dongle and what to consider when buying one. In general, however, these are fairly inexpensive, flexible ways to upgrade your laptop, and I’d recommend always carrying one in your laptop bag!

item.title: Still on Windows 11 24H2? You have one week to upgrade
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
If you’re still on Windows 11 24H2, time is running out. Microsoft is ending support for that version of Windows this month, so you’ll need to upgrade to either 25H2 or (ideally) 26H2 as soon as possible. If you don’t, you’ll put your system at increasing risk over time. Support for Windows 11 24H2 ends on October 13th, 2026 —less than a week from today. Once that deadline hits, you’ll no longer receive security, feature, or quality-of-life updates on your PC. How do you know if you’re still on 24H2? You can check by opening Windows Settings (use the Windows key + I keyboard shortcut), clicking “System” in the left panel, scrolling all the way down to “About” in the right panel, scrolling down to the “Windows specifications” section, and spotting what it says for “Version.” If you’re on 24H2, it’ll say “24H2.” (Also make note of “Edition,” which will likely be “Windows 11 Home” or “Windows 11 Pro.”) Microsoft explicitly states on this support page : Windows 11, version 24H2 Home and Pro editions will reach end of updates on October 13, 2026. Devices running these editions will no longer receive fixes for known issues, time zone updates, technical support, or monthly security and preview updates containing protections from the latest security threats. Enterprise and Education editions remain supported until October 12, 2027. In other words, the end of support will only affect PCs running Windows 11 Home or Pro editions. Windows 11 Enterprise and Education editions will get another year of support, ending on October 12th, 2027. This extra year is in line with Microsoft’s standard practice and isn’t specific to 24H2. Windows 11 26H2 is already available , so you should upgrade to that if you can. To do so, open Windows Settings again and navigate to “Windows Update” in the left panel, then enable the “Get the latest updates as soon as they’re available” option in the right panel. Then, wait until the Windows Update page shows “Windows 11, version 26H2 is available.” Even though the update has a few known issues for some users , it has some important optimizations that speed up Windows 11 performance on older hardware , so it’s worth taking the leap. That’s one of the areas in which Microsoft is indeed improving Windows 11. item.title: Building a PC in 2026 is all about choosing your compromises
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Anyone who wants or needs a new desktop computer has long had a choice to make: Buy a ready-built computer or build one yourself from individual components. The choice isn’t always that simple, and there are several factors that can make either option appealing. The price of a pre-built computer always includes, in one way or another, the cost of assembling it. If you build it yourself, you can spend all your money on getting the best possible components and pay for the assembly with your own time and by taking on the risk yourself. Build your own computer. Anere Lusina But building your own computer also offers incredible freedom and a sense of pride in what you can achieve yourself. It’s something that’s difficult to quantify in terms of money, but for many people, that’s the biggest draw. What does it mean to build a computer yourself? If you’ve never attempted to build a computer before, it can feel like a big and daunting task. But just like putting together an Ikea kitchen, it’s something the vast majority of people can manage if they just take the time and do their research. And unlike a kitchen, you don’t need to worry about any potential water leaks — at least, not unless you decide to build a system with water cooling! Building a computer basically involves three separate tasks: planning and buying components; fitting the components into the case; and configuring the BIOS, installing the operating system, and testing that everything works as it should. The first is the most complex, as there are so many components to choose from. Fortunately, you don’t need to learn and keep track of everything yourself, as there are plenty of websites with computer-building tools that help you put together components that are compatible with one another. Assembling the components isn’t actually that complicated, but you should definitely read a guide or two and watch a few YouTube videos that walk you through the whole process step by step. With video guides, for example, you can see how cable routing works in practice and pick up lots of little tips that make the build easier and safer. The same goes for learning about the BIOS and how to install Windows — familiarize yourself with these process before you begin. Advantages of building your own PC Total flexibility – you choose all the components. It can be very satisfying to use a computer you’ve built yourself. It’s usually cheaper. Plenty of scope for upgrading later. Disadvantages of building your own computer Choosing components is complicated and can take a lot of time. You take the risk that something might go wrong during the build. Advantages of buying a ready-built computer You get a ready-built computer without any risk or effort. You can find computers on sale, which can lower the overall price. Disadvantages of a pre-built computer It’s unlikely you’ll find a computer with exactly the combination of components you’d prefer. Many pre-built computers have an older processor, slightly slower memory, or some other compromise. What should I do if something goes wrong or breaks? It’s a good idea to order components so that they all arrive at the same time and you can assemble the computer within the standard return window. If any component were to malfunction, you could easily return and replace it without the hassle of making a warranty complaint. Should any component break later on, you can either contact the manufacturer or the seller for recourse under the product’s warranty. Cable management is an important but not particularly glamorous part of building a computer. Andrey Matveev Still, it is, of course, your own responsibility to assemble the computer safely. This means, among other things, that you must avoid discharging static electricity, but also ensure that components are fitted correctly. Some graphics cards are so heavy that they may need to be braced to avoid damaging the PCI Express slot, so read and follow all instructions carefully, both for the components and the case you have chosen. Computer builders A middle ground between buying a ready-built computer in a shop and building one yourself is to have a PC custom built by a vendor. For instance, boutique PC vendors such as iBuypower and Cyberpower will build a PC to your specification, taking care of the assembly and testing. But you’ll need to buy all the components from them, which of course doesn’t always give you the best price or choice. How to find your way through the component jungle If you enjoy getting deep into the details, you can, of course, take it upon yourself to keep track of all the components and ensure that the ones you choose are compatible with one another. However, most people choose to use a computer-building tool. The site PC Part Picker is the best known of these. With these tools, you can, for example, start with a specific case, a specific motherboard, or a specific graphics card. Once you have selected a component, the lists of other components are filtered to show only those that are compatible with your first choice, and the process continues in this way. If you try to select something that is not compatible with one of the other components you have chosen, you will receive a warning. Compatibility has two aspects: technical and physical. The technical aspect concerns, for example, whether a memory module fits a particular motherboard, or whether that motherboard supports a particular processor. A compact computer is more complicated to build and to select the right components for. Đào Hiếu In terms of size, it is simply a question of whether the components will fit inside the chosen chassis alongside the other selected components. Does the processor cooler protrude high enough above the memory modules to avoid interference when you choose high-performance memory with large built-in coolers? Will the long graphics card fit into the space inside the chassis? With a generously sized chassis and an ATX or E-ATX motherboard, you can usually fit almost anything in, but it’s still worth double-checking. And if you want to build a more compact computer in a small chassis with a Mini-ITX motherboard, the dimensions suddenly become very important. Which components are most important, and where can I cut corners? This depends on what you’ll be using the computer for, how you view future expansion options, and your sense of aesthetics. The graphics card is a key component, especially for gamers. Rafael Pol Graphics card If you’re looking to play high-end games with high graphics settings, the graphics card is undoubtedly the most important component, and you can cut corners on almost everything else to make room in your budget for it. If you can afford it, you’ll benefit greatly from choosing an AMD processor with so-called 3D V-Cache (indicated by ‘x3D’ at the end of the model name), such as the previous-generation Ryzen 5 7500X3D. The expanded cache means that gaming performance is less dependent on the speed of the main memory, so you can cut back there — something that can save you a fair bit of money given today’s memory prices. For anyone interested in running local AI, the graphics card is also important, but in this case it is primarily the amount of graphics memory that matters. And for AI, you can easily combine two cheaper graphics cards instead of one more expensive one, which isn’t possible for gaming. Be careful when inserting the processor into its socket. IT Services EU Processor For everyone else, the processor and graphics card are roughly equally important. My suggestion is that you choose one of the latest models, as they tend to be more efficient, feature the latest technologies, and will be fully supported by Windows for longer. Something to consider is whether you want to buy a processor and graphics card at roughly the same level, or opt for a slightly more powerful one and a slightly simpler one, with the aim of upgrading the latter at a later date. By opting for a cheaper graphics card, you can get a new, more powerful one in a couple of years’ time, while still benefiting from the slightly better processor you chose from the start. Memory and storage Most people won’t notice any practical difference between a blazing-fast SSD with PCIe 5.0 and a cheaper one with PCIe 4.0. When it comes to storage, a reliable manufacturer and a model that has received good reviews are more important than maximum speed, and you can save a fair bit by skipping the cutting-edge technology. When it comes to memory, capacity is the most important factor. Really fast memory is only important for a few specific use cases and is never worth it for the average user. If you’re using Windows, 16GB is the minimum you’ll need. Given today’s prices, it’s understandable if you want to save as much as possible on memory. Unless you know you’ll be running a great many programs simultaneously, or individual memory-intensive programs such as virtualized operating systems or Adobe Photoshop, 16GB should be enough. As long as your motherboard has four memory slots, you can always buy more later. Other components The case is something many people choose to skimp on, but this often means the computer looks less stylish and, perhaps more importantly, is more fiddly to build. Furthermore, it may have poorer airflow and, consequently, poorer heat dissipation, resulting in higher temperatures and lower performance. I would therefore recommend that you at least look at review ratings and choose a chassis that suits your needs, even if it costs a bit more. Another important component is the power supply unit; here, you need to ensure that its capacity is high enough for the components you’ve chosen, as well as any future upgrades you think you might need. Efficiency and noise levels are other factors worth bearing in mind. The power supply is important. Don’t skimp, but don’t go overboard either. Andrey Matveev For other components, you can often get by with cheaper models, but I recommend sticking to trusted brands and reading reviews. For example, there are some really good, inexpensive CPU coolers, but also a few real duds. These recommendations obviously apply even if you choose to buy a pre-built computer — don’t just focus on the processor, graphics card, and memory; check the case, power supply, and other components as well. What initially seems like a bargain can soon turn into an expensive lesson if you have to upgrade several components. Don’t forget future expandability When comparing a pre-built computer — whether it’s a traditional tower model with standard components, a mini-PC or something more exotic — with one you build yourself, you shouldn’t overlook the possibilities for expanding and upgrading the computer in the future. If you build it yourself, for example, you can choose two larger memory modules instead of four smaller ones. It’ll be more expensive now, but you can buy more later. In most pre-built systems, all the memory slots are filled, unless you buy a very small amount of memory. A mini-PC rarely has more than two slots, and many have soldered-on memory that can neither be expanded nor replaced with larger modules. Upgrade your computer with more memory, storage, or a new processor. Andrey Matveev Storage can almost always be replaced, but in tower models and home-built machines there are usually empty M.2 slots that you can fill without having to replace the existing storage. With a traditional tower computer, there may be spare PCI Express slots that you can use for additional storage, new network cards or other components you may later realise you need. This applies whether you buy a ready-built system or build it yourself, but the number of slots available varies greatly from one motherboard to another. Ten years ago, it was common to have several spare slots, but nowadays many manufacturers choose to focus on more M.2 slots for SSDs, and sometimes there’s only one extra slot apart from the one intended for the graphics card. Or not even that. Compare the total cost Corner. Andre Tan If you’re mainly looking to get as much computer as possible for your money, I suggest you look at both pre-built computers and the various components you’ve selected. Don’t forget to add a Windows licence if you need one, and any peripherals such as a monitor, mouse, and keyboard. Then compare the total price. Only then can you decide whether the lower cost, the better components or the greater upgrade potential are worth the effort. Related content 5 mistakes to avoid when buying a PC case Building a PC?
